title: WebMCP: Browser Tools with Shared UI State

defaults.structure: One hands-on talk around WebMCP and three demos

slides.title:
Your website
has tools, too.
slides.subtitle:
WebMCP: Expose your web app's functions
to AI agents without duplicating your UI.
slides.speaker: Sebastián Gómez · Google Developer Expert (Web Technologies)
notes:
A web page already knows how to search, filter, and prepare a reading route. How can we offer those same actions to an agent while preserving an interface that a person understands? This talk starts with a concrete need: choosing what to read before a talk.

Set the scope: WebMCP is still experimental. The demos include a local console for exploring the same functions when the browser does not expose the API. That console is not an AI agent.

slides.title:
From DOM scraping
to schema contracts.
slides.subtitle: The agent invokes a typed function; the user keeps visual control of the page.

diagram.title: 1. User
diagram.body: States the goal and inspects changes directly in the page UI.

diagram.title: 2. WebMCP Tool
diagram.body: Accepts validated arguments (add_to_route) without brittle DOM selectors.

diagram.title: 3. Shared Page State
diagram.body: Updates the on-screen list and allows one-click removal.

notes: A person wants to prepare for a talk. The intention is simple: help me choose what to read. The experience should remain understandable on screen.
The agent needs a bounded action, such as adding an article. A tool with defined arguments reduces what the agent must infer about the page.
The visible list changes. The person can inspect the result and remove an article with the usual controls. That continuity is the central idea.

slides.title:
One callback for both
the UI and the agent.
slides.subtitle: The DOM button and document.modelContext invoke the exact same function.

diagram.title: UI Event (click)
diagram.body: User clicks “Add” on the article card.

diagram.title: addToRoute(args)
diagram.body: Validates ID, prevents duplicates, and re-renders the view.

diagram.title: registerTool({ execute })
diagram.body: Browser invokes the exact same application callback.

notes: The add button calls an application function. We do not need to build a second application for the agent.
That function validates the identifier, avoids duplicates, and updates the list. State and rules remain the application's responsibility.
The tool callback uses that same function. The browser connection is a small layer around logic that already makes sense to the person.

slides.title:
Shared State:
add_to_route.
slides.subtitle: Add via the WebMCP tool, remove via the DOM button.
steps: Call add_to_route with {"articleId":"models"} and verify the counter increments to 1.
Remove that article using the DOM “Remove” button to confirm both share the same state array.
Pass {"articleId":"missing"} and inspect the structured UNKNOWN_ARTICLE error (retryable: true).
notes:
Open Reading Route. Explain that the catalog metadata is curated sample content. First add Small models from the local console with articleId models. The visible route receives the article. Then remove that same article with the ordinary button.

Try an unknown identifier to show a useful error. The console calls the function directly; it does not simulate language understanding. With a prepared WebMCP browser, inspect the registered tool or use a compatible agent.

Contingency: if the agent or API is unavailable, continue with the console and explain the difference explicitly. The demo checks the contract and shared state.

slides.title:
Structured errors
with retryable.
slides.subtitle: Return a stable error code so the caller can self-correct.
stepCallouts: Reject unknown IDs before mutating state and return a stable error code.
Specify how to fix the argument and set retryable: true.
notes: This is an excerpt of Reading Route's error response. article is the result of looking up the supplied identifier. When it is absent, the function returns an object without changing the route. UNKNOWN_ARTICLE is a stable application code, not a universal error shape defined by WebMCP.

The message explains recovery and retryable tells the client that it can correct the arguments. It does not require an automatic retry. The application also rejects incorrect argument types and avoids duplicates. The source link contains the full implementation and its more detailed messages.

slides.title:
Registering on
modelContext.
slides.subtitle: Stable name, enum-constrained inputSchema, and the shared add callback.
stepCallouts: Provide name and description so the agent knows when to select the tool.
Constrain articleId with a JSON Schema enum built from live catalog IDs.
Pass the application's add function directly to execute.
notes: This registration uses document.modelContext.registerTool and awaits its promise. add_to_route is a stable name; the description explains when to select the tool. This excerpt assumes support was already detected. We will cover that check and registration errors later.

The schema helper belongs to this application: it builds an object schema, requires its properties, and disallows extra fields. articles is the demo catalog; its identifiers bound articleId. We will see the helper body on the contract slide. These dependencies are in the linked full source.

execute receives add, the same application callback used by the button. In the demo, add validates arguments, avoids duplicates, and renders the route again. The browser API supplies the entry point; rules and state remain in the application.

slides.title:
Explicit confirmation
before execution.
slides.subtitle: The tool stages the request; the human click resolves the Promise.
steps: Stage a request for 2 tickets: the review panel updates while the confirmed ledger remains empty.
Click “Reject” to verify the tool Promise resolves as rejected with zero side effects.
Stage again and click “Confirm”: only the user's click event commits the state change.
notes:
Open The Last Click. All tickets are fictional: no booking, payment, or request to an external service occurs. Prepare two tickets and show that no confirmed request exists. Reject the proposal.

Prepare another request and confirm it with the visible button. Local history changes only after that decision. An annotation describes the action for the tool-consuming client; the application must still enforce its own review boundary.

With a prepared WebMCP client, show the tool requesting review. Never present a client's warning as a guaranteed feature of every agent.

slides.title:
Pending Promise
until confirmed.
slides.subtitle: consequentialHint informs the client; the Promise enforces the gate.
builds: The rule lives in the application
stepCallouts: consequentialHint: true is descriptive metadata, not an access control.
new Promise pauses execution until the UI button calls finishReview.
notes: The Last Click registers requestReview with these annotations. consequentialHint describes a consequence without granting permission or imposing identical confirmation behavior across clients. This is an excerpt: the full registration passes the annotation object alongside the name, description, schema, and callback.

Application code enforces review. prepare validates quantity and pending requests, updates the screen, and can return an error. On the valid path, the promise stays pending until a person decides. In the full source, the confirmation button resolves finishReview; the rejection button returns rejected. The full flow also checks for a pending request, handles AbortSignal, cleans up state, and records the result. No payment or real booking occurs.

slides.title:
readOnlyHint &
debugging annotations.
slides.subtitle: Tag diagnostic tools separately from user-facing actions.
stepCallouts: Expose a read-only state snapshot for debugging internal state.
Set readOnlyHint: true and debugging: true to separate diagnostic tools.
notes: This excerpt defines inspect_state with an empty schema and a read callback. inspectState stands for the demo callback returning a snapshot with time and proposal count; it is application logic, not another browser API. Register this tool using the same registration pattern we just saw.

readOnlyHint describes read-only behavior and debugging identifies a development audience. Neither annotation is an access control. The observatory explicitly filters these tools; that illustrates this console's decision and does not guarantee every agent's behavior.

slides.title:
Inspecting schemas,
errors, and traces.
slides.subtitle: Distinguish validation errors, JSON syntax failures, and debug tools.
steps: Call find_demo with {"query":"browser"} and inspect its inputSchema, annotations, and latency.
Compare {"query":""} (structured INVALID_QUERY error) against malformed JSON (SyntaxError).
Enable “Include debugging: true tools” to reveal and execute inspect_state.
notes:
Open Tool Observatory. Execute find_demo with query browser. Show the schema and result. Then use an empty argument to show a recoverable error. Finally try malformed JSON to distinguish an editor error from the tool's result.

Enable Include developer tools. Select inspect_state and change the arguments to an empty object. This console's filter illustrates the debugging audience; it does not establish every agent's behavior. If native WebMCP is available, inspect the browser registrations.

slides.title:
Input validation
with JSON Schema.
slides.subtitle: Required properties and additionalProperties: false.
stepCallouts: Build an object JSON Schema from the declared property map.
Mark all keys as required and reject undeclared fields.
Pair declarative schema bounds with runtime checks in your callback.
notes: This is the schema helper used to register add_to_route. It takes a property map and returns an object JSON Schema. It is a small application function, not a function that WebMCP adds to the browser.

Object.keys makes every supplied property required and additionalProperties: false rejects unexpected names. The enum in the registration bounds article identifiers. The contract guides the client, but add still validates real input before modifying state; types and schemas do not replace business rules.

Test null, incorrect types, unknown identifiers, and duplicates as well as the successful path. In the review flow, test rejection and confirmation too. The source link shows runtime validation alongside this helper.

slides.title:
Feature detection
& UI fallback.
slides.subtitle: Render the UI first; register only when registerTool exists.
stepCallouts: Render standard DOM controls before checking for WebMCP support.
Catch registration errors without breaking the user interface.
notes: The first line renders ordinary controls before attempting registration. render, tool, and status are application pieces. This excerpt runs in an async context, like the demo's registration helper. Without WebMCP support, the page already lets people add and remove readings.

Check document.modelContext and registerTool. If the method exists, await its promise before announcing a registered tool. The reviewed local setup uses enable-webmcp-testing; documentation also describes the origin trial. Support detection concerns the browser actually being tested.

The catch reports registration failure without removing page buttons. A useful interface must survive both missing support and failed registration. WebMCP connects tools to the page; an agent may use local or remote inference, and registration cannot establish where its model runs.

slides.title:
Document-context
boundaries.
slides.subtitle: WebMCP tools exist only while the document is open in an active tab.

specs.detail: document.modelContext exposes tools on the active document, not as a headless background MCP server.
Every tool invocation updates visible state so the user can inspect or undo via standard DOM controls.
Registering a tool defines the browser interface; the calling agent may run locally or in the cloud.

notes: The reviewed design describes tools living in a page context. That guides the experiences worth building.

The documentation describes discovery limits and flows without a human interface. Future explorations exist, but this use case does not need them. Avoid promising global discovery or background tasks from today's example.

slides.title:
Exposing your first
WebMCP tool.
slides.subtitle: Wrap an existing UI handler in three concrete steps.

specs.detail: Extract the function that already filters, searches, or updates state from your click/submit listeners.
Declare strict types, enum arrays for known IDs, required keys, and additionalProperties: false.
When a tool commits or mutates critical state, keep the returned Promise pending until user confirmation.

notes: Choose an action a person already wants on your site. Write down what it accepts and changes. Connect it to the ordinary control, then to a tool. Test the complete journey before expanding the catalog. A reading route is a good first candidate for my site.

slides.title:
Single state for both
the UI and agent tools.
slides.subtitle: Strict schemas, human confirmation gates, and progressive enhancement.

specs.detail: The DOM button and registerTool({ execute }) invoke the exact same validation and state logic.
consequentialHint, readOnlyHint, and debugging are descriptive hints; your app enforces security.
When document.modelContext is absent, the application remains 100% functional via standard controls.

notes: This talk offers a practical connection: tools can reuse rules that already make an interface valuable. The examples and source review are in the local gallery. Primary sources also appear in the presentation notes.

slides.title:
Which function in your app
would you expose first?
slides.subtitle: Interactive demos, source code, and technical references.
notes: Reserve two and a half minutes for questions. If nobody asks immediately, invite an example of a real audience action and walk through its goal, arguments, validation, and visible result. Do not promise version support without checking its documentation. To inspect the code, return to the gallery and open any of the three demos.
